Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: Severe headaches with episodes of feeling hot; associated autonomic and systemic symptoms.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began after changing jobs; episodes are intermittent and occur mainly during work; timing varies (one issue at a time, not simultaneous).
- Headache characteristics: Frontal/around-head location; sometimes localized to the front; associated nausea; no clear progression described.
- Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath (at desk, with exertion unclear); tachycardia (feeling heart beating fast); tingling in both arms; reduced appetite; unintentional weight loss (~5 lb); decreased libido.
- Triggers/setting: Occur during work (meetings, laptop use, computer work); stress level high (approximately 7–8/10).
- Past medical history: Hyperthyroidism; on thyroxine; adherent.
- Medications: Thyroxine (dose not documented).
- Allergies: No allergies reported.
- Social history: Lawyer in London; alcohol use weekly (a couple of glasses of wine); does not smoke; no illicit drug use.
- Other: No prior similar headaches reported; no fever or sinus symptoms noted.

Assessment & Plan:
1) Headache with systemic/autonomic symptoms in a patient with known hyperthyroidism
- Assessment: Likely etiologies include thyrotoxicosis/hyperthyroidism–related symptoms and possibly a primary headache disorder (migraine/tension-type) with autonomic features; symptoms correlate with work-related stress and prolonged computer use; hyperthyroid symptoms are supported by tachycardia, weight loss, heat intolerance, decreased appetite, and libido change.
- Differential diagnosis (consistent with DDx): 
  - Thyrotoxicosis / Hyperthyroidism due to levothyroxine therapy (high likelihood)
  - Migraine-type or tension-type headache with associated autonomic symptoms (medium-high likelihood)
  - Anxiety/panic–related autonomic symptoms (medium likelihood)
  - Less likely: pheochromocytoma (low likelihood)
- Investigations planned: In-clinic physical exam (cardiovascular and respiratory); blood tests with emphasis on thyroxine level to assess thyroid status.
- Treatment plan: No new medications at this time; proceed with in-person evaluation and lab results to guide management.
- Referrals: Not indicated at this time; reassess after initial clinic evaluation and labs.

2) Hyperthyroidism / thyrotoxicosis evaluation and management
- Assessment: Hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis remains a coherent explanation given known history and symptom cluster; iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis (levothyroxine over-replacement) is a plausible contributor.
- Differential diagnosis (consistent with DDx): 
  - Thyrotoxicosis / Hyperthyroidism (high)
  - Graves’ disease or autoimmune thyroiditis (could contribute but patient is on replacement therapy)
  - Other endocrine/metabolic causes if labs do not fit thyroid picture
- Investigations planned: Thyroxine level measurement (and plan to interpret in the context of symptoms); possibly additional thyroid function testing as needed after results.
- Treatment plan: Adjust levothyroxine dosing as indicated by lab results and clinical response.
- Referrals: Endocrinology referral not currently indicated; follow after lab results and clinical course.
